title: even
subtitle: even the bathroom / she's even been to the Antarctic / even earlier / even though
summary: Use even to say that something is unusual or surprising, put it in the right place with the verb, use even + comparative, and use even though / even if with a subject and verb.

lesson.heading: Something unusual or surprising
lesson.text: Tina loves watching TV. She has a television in every room of the house, **even the bathroom**. We use **even** to say that something is unusual or surprising. It is not usual to have a television in the bathroom.

examples.text: These pictures are really awful. **Even I** take better pictures than these.
examples.note: and I'm certainly not a good photographer

examples.text: He always wears a coat, **even in hot weather**.
The print was very small. I couldn't read it, **even with glasses**.
Nobody would help her, **not even her best friend**. or **Not even her best friend** would help her.

lesson.heading: even with the verb
lesson.text: You can use **even** with the verb in the middle of a sentence. You can also use even with a negative: **not even, can't even, don't even** etc.

examples.text: Laura has travelled all over the world. She's **even been** to the Antarctic.
They are very rich. They **even have** their own private jet.
I can't cook. I **can't even boil** an egg.
examples.note: and boiling an egg is very easy

examples.text: They weren't very friendly to us. They **didn't even say** hello.
Jessica is very fit. She's been running quite fast and she's **not even out of breath**.

lesson.heading: even + comparative
lesson.text: You can use **even** + comparative (cheaper / more expensive etc.) to say that something is more than you already expected.

examples.text: I got up very early, but Jack got up **even earlier**.
I knew I didn't have much money, but I have **even less** than I thought.
We were very surprised to get an email from her. We were **even more surprised** when she came to see us a few days later.

lesson.heading: even though / even when / even if
lesson.text: We use **even though / even when / even if** + subject + verb. We do not use even + subject + verb on its own.

examples.text: **Even though** Tina can't drive, she has a car.
He never shouts, **even when** he's angry.
This river is dangerous. It's dangerous to swim in it, **even if** you're a strong swimmer.
I can't reach the shelf **even if** I stand on a chair.
The river is dangerous, **even for** strong swimmers.

left.label: even if
left.text: It doesn't matter what happens - the result is the same.
examples: We're going to the beach tomorrow. It doesn't matter what the weather is like. We're going **even if** the weather is bad.

right.label: if
right.text: The result depends on the condition.
examples: We want to go to the beach tomorrow, but we won't go **if** the weather is bad.

lesson.text: Before a subject + verb you need even though, even when or even if - never even alone: even though she can't drive (not ~~even she can't drive~~).

exercises.prompt: Kate usually hates hotels. On holiday the three friends stayed at a hotel and everybody liked it, ___.
exercises.explanation: It is surprising that Kate liked it, because she usually hates hotels: even Kate.

exercises.prompt: Amy is very interested in art. The friends went to an art gallery, but nobody enjoyed it, ___.
exercises.explanation: Nobody enjoyed it, and it is surprising that Amy didn't either: not even Amy.

exercises.prompt: Lisa is almost always late. The friends arranged to meet and they all arrived on time, ___.
exercises.explanation: Everybody was on time, and it is surprising that Lisa was too: even Lisa.

exercises.prompt: Rachel has met lots of famous people. Say that this includes the prime minister.
exercises.answer: She's even met the prime minister.
exercises.explanation: Even goes with the verb in the middle of the sentence: She's even met ...

exercises.prompt: I can't remember anything about her. Say that this includes her name.
exercises.answer: I can't even remember her name.

exercises.prompt: The church is 700 years old, but the house next to it is ___.
The first question was very difficult to answer. The second one was ___.
exercises.explanation: Even + comparative with a long adjective: even more difficult.

exercises.prompt: Neither of us was hungry. I ate very little and my friend ate ___.
exercises.explanation: The comparative of little is less: even less.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the sentence that follows it.

pairs.right: She has a television in every room, even the bathroom.
He can't even boil an egg.
They even have their own private jet.

pairs.left: Laura has travelled all over the world.
pairs.right: She's even been to the Antarctic.

pairs.left: They weren't very friendly to us.

exercises.prompt: The bus leaves in five minutes, but we can still catch it ___ we run.
exercises.explanation: Catching the bus depends on running, so this is a real condition: if we run.

exercises.prompt: The bus leaves in two minutes. We won't catch it now ___ we run.
exercises.explanation: Running makes no difference to the result, so: even if we run.

exercises.prompt: Mark's Spanish isn't very good, ___ after three years in Spain.
exercises.explanation: There is no subject + verb after the gap, only a phrase (after three years), so even alone is correct.

exercises.statement: Even she can't drive, she has a car.
exercises.explanation: Even though she can't drive, she has a car. Before subject + verb we need even though, not even alone.

exercises.statement: I couldn't sleep even though I was very tired.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Even though + subject + verb (I was very tired) is the right form.
